## The problem

Sometimes you know, before seeing any data, that certain correlations are exactly zero —
a graphical structure, a confirmatory factor model, a physical constraint. You cannot just
sample a correlation matrix from an LKJ prior and zero out cells: the result is generally
not positive definite. The zeros have to be built into the parameterization itself.

This post races twelve Stan parameterizations of "LKJ prior + hard zeros" against each
other. All twelve target the same posterior (verified against each other within Monte
Carlo error), so the comparison is purely about sampling geometry: divergences, effective
sample size, and cost per gradient evaluation.

The punchline: the two families of solutions make opposite trade-offs, and a hybrid —
an exact-constraint subspace construction with a canonical triangular basis — gets the
best of both: **zero divergences across every run and the best ESS per gradient in the
field**.

## Family 1: forced zeros

The construction I first saw from Bob Carpenter walks the Cholesky factor
row by row. Writing $\Omega = L L'$ with unit-norm rows of $L$, the correlation in cell
$(i,j)$ is

$$
\Omega_{ij} = b_1 + L_{ij} L_{jj}, \qquad
b_1 = \sum_{k<j} L_{ik} L_{jk},
$$

so a structural zero pins $L_{ij} = -b_1 / L_{jj}$ — no parameter needed. Conditioning
the LKJ distribution on $\Omega_{ij} = 0$ (a delta function in $\Omega$ coordinates)
contributes a density correction $-\log L_{jj}$ per zero.

```{.stan}
if (is_zero(i, j, zeros, zero_idx)) {
  real b = dot_product(L[j, 1:(j - 1)], L[i, 1:(j - 1)]);
  L[i, j] = -b / L[j, j];   // implies Omega[i, j] == 0
  jacobian += -log(L[j, j]);
  zero_idx += 1;
}
```

The forced-zero trick composes with essentially any Cholesky-style parameterization of
the free cells. I tested eight members of this family:

| label | free-cell parameterization |
|---|---|
| `carpenter` | direct Cholesky entries, bounded by the remaining stick |
| `pinkney` | correlation-scale value divided by $L_{jj}$, multiplicative stick |
| `ldl` / `ldl2` / `ldl3` | $LDL'$ factorization; stick tracked by `log_diff_exp`, `log1m`-ratio, or natural scale |
| `cvine` | C-vine partial correlations with the LKJ Beta factorization |
| `rowscale` | direct Cholesky entries, row-scaling stick |
| `schur` | canonical partial correlations, $L_{ij} = r \tanh(x)$ |

They all share one flaw. The forced value $-b_1/L_{jj}$ can exceed the row's remaining
stick, $\sqrt{1 - \sum_{k<j} L_{ik}^2}$. When it does, a downstream `sqrt` of a negative
number produces `NaN`, the proposal is rejected, and near that boundary the sampler
diverges. Every member of the family runs at roughly a **1% divergence rate** on the test
patterns below — a bias risk you have to manage with `adapt_delta` forever.

The three LDL variants deserve a footnote: they define *identical* densities and differ
only in floating-point arithmetic, yet their divergence totals span 356–466. That spread
is a direct measurement of the noise floor for single-fit divergence counts, and it is
wider than most gaps between genuinely different parameterizations. Beware of divergence
league tables built from single runs.

## Family 2: exact-constraint subspaces

The second idea eliminates the boundary entirely. I learned it from **Seth Axen**, in a
[Turing.jl discussion on positive definite matrices with structural
zeros](https://github.com/TuringLang/Turing.jl/discussions/2067):

> For each column j, each column i for i < j that is orthogonal to column j decreases the
> dimensionality of the hemisphere by 1. So we simply construct a point on a lower
> dimensional hemisphere and use the QR decomposition of the orthogonal columns to lift it
> to a higher dimensional hemisphere.

Row $i$ of a correlation Cholesky factor is a unit vector with positive last coordinate.
Because row $j$ is zero beyond column $j$, the constraint $\Omega_{ij}=0$ says row $i$ is
**orthogonal to row $j$ as a whole vector**. So a row with $n_z$ zeros lives on a unit
hemisphere inside the orthogonal complement of its zero-partner rows — a sphere of
dimension $d = i - 1 - n_z$. Sample there and the constraint holds *by construction*:
no proposal can ever be infeasible, so the divergence mechanism of Family 1 does not
exist. The joint delta over a row's zeros contributes
$-\tfrac{1}{2}\log\det(A'A)$, where $A$ collects the zero-partner rows — Axen's
"divide by the determinant of the R factor."

My first two implementations (`qr`, `qr2`) followed the recipe literally: Householder QR
of $A$, complement basis from the full $Q$, hemisphere chart via a gnomonic map or tanh
sticks. They achieved exactly zero divergences — and about **40% of the ESS** of the
forced-zero family. The chart didn't matter; the basis did. Householder's complement
columns are an arbitrary orthonormal frame that *spins* as the earlier rows move, so the
raw coordinates keep changing meaning underneath the sampler.

## The fix: a canonical triangular basis (`tri`)

Replace the QR basis with one anchored to the matrix entries. For each free column $k$ of
row $i$, take $e_k$ and fill in the row's forced columns by back-substitution through the
zero constraints — Carpenter's fill applied to *basis vectors* instead of the sampled row.
Collect these as the columns of $T$. Splitting coordinates into forced ($Z$) and free
($F$) sets, $T_F = I$ and $T_Z = -(A_Z')^{-1} A_F'$, and orthonormalizing costs one small
Cholesky: with $S = \operatorname{chol}(T'T)$, the map $v = T S'^{-T} z$ satisfies
$\lVert v \rVert = \lVert z \rVert$, so the sphere-measure bookkeeping is unchanged.

Two pleasant identities finish the job. First, because the zero-partner rows have
triangular support, $A_Z$ is triangular with the partners' diagonals on its diagonal, and
Sylvester's determinant identity gives

$$
\det(A'A) \;=\; \Big(\prod_{j \in Z} L_{jj}\Big)^{2} \, \det(T'T),
$$

so the delta term splits into Carpenter's $-\sum_j \log L_{jj}$ — which now falls out
*analytically*, no linear algebra required — plus $-\sum_k \log S_{kk}$, which rides
along free with the orthonormalization Cholesky. Second, since $T_F = I$, the Gram is
$T'T = I + W'W$ with $W$ just the $n_z$ forced-coordinate rows, so the crossprod works on
length-$n_z$ vectors. Per constrained row, the entire construction costs one $d \times d$
Cholesky and some small matrix-vector products. No QR anywhere.

```{.stan filename="unitvec-tri-corr-zeros.stan"}
functions {
  matrix cholesky_corr_constrain_tri_jacobian(int K, vector raw,
                                              array[,] int zeros) {
    matrix[K, K] L = rep_matrix(0, K, K);
    int raw_idx = 1;
    int zero_idx = 1;
    L[1, 1] = 1;

    for (i in 2:K) {
      int n_z = 0;
      while (zero_idx + n_z <= size(zeros)
             && zeros[zero_idx + n_z, 1] == i) {
        n_z += 1;
      }
      int d = i - 1 - n_z;

      // subsphere coordinates via tanh sticks (cosh-form jacobian)
      vector[d] z;
      real r = 1;
      for (k in 1:d) {
        real x = raw[raw_idx];
        real cosh_x = cosh(x);
        z[k] = r * tanh(x);
        jacobian += -(d - k + 2) * log(cosh_x);
        r /= cosh_x;
        raw_idx += 1;
      }

      if (n_z == 0) {
        if (d > 0) {
          L[i, 1:d] = z';
        }
        L[i, i] = r;
      } else {
        array[n_z] int zc;
        for (m in 1:n_z) {
          zc[m] = zeros[zero_idx + m - 1, 2];
        }

        // the joint-delta term -0.5 * log det(Gram of zero-partner rows)
        // factors: det(A'A) = prod(L[j,j])^2 * det(T'T) by Sylvester
        for (m in 1:n_z) {
          jacobian += -log(L[zc[m], zc[m]]);
        }

        if (d > 0) {
          array[d] int free_cols;
          {
            int fc = 0;
            int zp = 1;
            for (c in 1:(i - 1)) {
              if (zp <= n_z && zc[zp] == c) {
                zp += 1;
              } else {
                fc += 1;
                free_cols[fc] = c;
              }
            }
          }
          // triangular basis: unit at each free column, forced columns
          // filled by back-substitution so every column is orthogonal to
          // the zero-partner rows
          matrix[i - 1, d] T = rep_matrix(0, i - 1, d);
          for (k in 1:d) {
            int col = free_cols[k];
            T[col, k] = 1;
            for (m in 1:n_z) {
              int j = zc[m];
              if (j > col) {
                T[j, k] = -dot_product(L[j, 1:(j - 1)], T[1:(j - 1), k])
                          / L[j, j];
              }
            }
          }
          // T's free-column rows are the identity, so T'T = I + W'W with
          // W the forced-column rows only
          matrix[n_z, d] W;
          for (m in 1:n_z) {
            W[m, ] = T[zc[m], ];
          }
          matrix[d, d] S = cholesky_decompose(add_diag(crossprod(W), 1.0));
          jacobian += -sum(log(diagonal(S)));
          vector[d] t = mdivide_right_tri_low(z', S)';
          L[i, 1:(i - 1)] = (T * t)';
        }
        L[i, i] = r;
        zero_idx += n_z;
      }
    }
    return L;
  }
}
data {
  int<lower=2> K;
  real<lower=0> eta;
  int<lower=0, upper=choose(K, 2)> N_zero;
  array[N_zero, 2] int zeros;  // lower triangular, row major order
}
parameters {
  vector[choose(K, 2) - N_zero] raw;
}
transformed parameters {
  matrix[K, K] L_Omega = cholesky_corr_constrain_tri_jacobian(K, raw, zeros);
}
model {
  L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(eta);
}
generated quantities {
  matrix[K, K] Omega = multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L_Omega);
}
```

I also tried a "donut" variant — one extra parameter per row, normalizing a free vector
instead of using a compact chart. It kept the exact-constraint geometry but the
$|u_{\text{last}}|$ fold put a power-law barrier at the equator and it diverged worse
than anything else in the field (2,531 total). Not every overparameterization trick
transfers.

## Results

Setup: $K = 7$, $\eta = 4$, prior-only, five random zero patterns (about half of the 21
lower-triangular cells zeroed, seeds 1–5), 4 chains $\times$ 2000 draws after 1000
warmup, default `adapt_delta = 0.8`, CmdStan 2.39. Correctness was checked on a separate
pattern: all twelve posteriors match the `carpenter` baseline within Monte Carlo error
(max free-cell mean difference $\le 0.008$ at bulk ESS $\ge$ 3,700), and the constrained
cells are numerically exact zeros ($\sim 10^{-19}$).

**Divergences** out of 8,000 post-warmup transitions:

| pattern | carpenter | pinkney | ldl | ldl2 | cvine | rowscale | ldl3 | schur | qr | qr2 | tri | donut |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| seed 1 | 34 | 53 | 53 | 26 | 41 | 44 | 40 | 40 | 0 | 0 | **0** | 522 |
| seed 2 | 61 | 65 | 74 | 107 | 64 | 78 | 104 | 60 | 0 | 0 | **0** | 551 |
| seed 3 | 77 | 44 | 67 | 57 | 69 | 44 | 68 | 59 | 0 | 0 | **0** | 500 |
| seed 4 | 137 | 157 | 130 | 112 | 186 | 155 | 152 | 123 | 0 | 0 | **0** | 418 |
| seed 5 | 110 | 94 | 114 | 54 | 141 | 114 | 102 | 29 | 0 | 0 | **0** | 540 |
| **total** | 419 | 413 | 438 | 356 | 501 | 435 | 466 | 311 | **0** | **0** | **0** | 2531 |

**Min bulk ESS** over the free cells of $\Omega$ (8,000 draws):

| pattern | carpenter | pinkney | ldl | ldl2 | cvine | rowscale | ldl3 | schur | qr | qr2 | tri | donut |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| seed 1 | 11639 | 10566 | 9979 | 10618 | 10219 | 11319 | 9840 | 11036 | 3995 | 3362 | **11430** | 4321 |
| seed 2 | 10817 | 9866 | 10826 | 9772 | 10188 | 10153 | 10361 | 10040 | 4049 | 3728 | **11427** | 5049 |
| seed 3 | 9344 | 11014 | 10244 | 10314 | 10946 | 9420 | 10625 | 10787 | 4334 | 4304 | 9574 | 3795 |
| seed 4 | 8395 | 9159 | 8326 | 9257 | 8771 | 9463 | 8266 | 9458 | 3701 | 3815 | **9582** | 5121 |
| seed 5 | 10381 | 10010 | 9268 | 8760 | 10301 | 9218 | 9896 | 4770 | 4267 | 4153 | **11284** | 4454 |
| **median** | 10381 | 10010 | 9979 | 9772 | 10219 | 9463 | 9896 | 10040 | 4049 | 3815 | **11284** | 4454 |

**Efficiency** (medians over the five patterns):

| | carpenter | pinkney | ldl | ldl2 | cvine | rowscale | ldl3 | schur | qr | qr2 | tri | donut |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| min ESS / 1000 gradients | 188.5 | 179.6 | 185.9 | 182.2 | 188.9 | 176.3 | 182.1 | 182.0 | 75.0 | 72.5 | **207.3** | 18.7 |
| total wall clock, 5 fits (s) | 4.53 | 4.10 | 4.40 | 4.51 | 5.14 | 4.21 | 4.51 | 4.15 | 2.07 | 2.06 | **1.95** | 9.72 |

The `tri` column is the whole story: zero divergences on every pattern, the highest
median ESS in the table, the best ESS per gradient evaluation, and the lowest wall-clock
time. The subspace family's short trajectories (no boundary to fight) plus a
well-anchored basis means it wins on *every* axis at once — the usual
robustness-versus-speed trade simply dissolves.

## Caveats

- Everything above is $K = 7$, $\eta = 4$, prior-only, dense zero patterns. Larger $K$,
  data likelihoods, and sparse patterns may reorder the forced-zero family — though the
  structural argument for `tri` (no infeasible region exists) is dimension-independent.
- Divergence counts from single fits are noisy; the identical-density LDL trio spans
  356–466 on the same patterns. The forced-vs-subspace gap (hundreds vs. exactly zero) is
  far outside that noise; the within-family rankings are not.
- The `tri` construction needs the zero list sorted in row-major order and one
  $d \times d$ `cholesky_decompose` per constrained row per gradient — negligible at this
  size, worth profiling at $K \gtrsim 50$.

## Attribution

The exact-constraint subspace idea — zeros as orthogonality constraints, sampling on a
lower-dimensional hemisphere and lifting through the orthogonal complement, with the
$\det R$ Jacobian factor — is due to [Seth Axen](https://sethaxen.com/), from
[TuringLang/Turing.jl discussion #2067](https://github.com/TuringLang/Turing.jl/discussions/2067).
The `tri` model is that idea with a different (canonical, triangular) choice of
complement basis and the determinant factored analytically.

The forced-zero construction and its $-\log L_{jj}$ conditioning correction I learned
from Bob Carpenter. The bounded/constrained Cholesky machinery used by several of the
Family-1 variants is described in my
[short note on flexible Cholesky parameterizations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.07286).
